definition.text: An online service where people store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link.

facts.text: Pastebins were developed in the late 1990s for IRC chatrooms about computing, where large blocks of computer output would disrupt closely interleaved conversation.
Chat users who post big blocks are often warned to use a pastebin instead or risk being banned from the service.
Account holders can store multiple text entries, called pastes, usually edit or delete them at any time, and on many platforms mark them public or private.
Pastebins may add commenting, rendering of markup such as Markdown or ReStructuredText, or version control.
The best-known pastebin is pastebin.com, created in 2002; many similar sites exist, and several open source pastebin applications can be self-hosted.
After the pastebin.pl pastebin was used for a data breach, Pastebin started monitoring the site for illegally pasted data, which drew a backlash from Anonymous.
The System Design Primer treats a pastebin design as like a Bit.ly design, except that it must store the paste contents instead of the original unshortened url.

title: Base62 encoding

definition.text: A way of writing numbers with 62 symbols, the digits and both cases of the English letters, so the result is safe to use in a URL.

facts.text: Base62 uses the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the numbers 0-9, that is 26 + 26 + 10 symbols.
Its output stays within [a-zA-Z0-9], which suits urls without escaping special characters; Base 64 is popular but its extra + and / characters cause trouble in urls.
N characters give 62^N possible values: 7 characters give ~3.5 trillion different URLs.
Base62 is deterministic, with no randomness. Singh notes that encoding the original URL this way is simple but does not guarantee non-duplicate or collision-resistant keys.

title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation

definition.text: A rough usage calculation, run in an interview if the interviewer wants it, that turns monthly request counts into per-second rates with round conversion figures.

facts.text: The primer advises clarifying with the interviewer whether to run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations at all.
Its handy conversion guide counts 2.5 million seconds per month, so 1 request per second is 2.5 million requests per month.
The same guide pairs 40 requests per second with 100 million requests per month, and 400 requests per second with 1 billion requests per month.

facts.text: Users paste text to get a random link and open links to view pastes. Pastes do not expire by default but can be timed. The service tracks monthly visit stats, deletes expired pastes and stays highly available.
Out of scope: registering an account, verifying email, logging in, editing the document, setting visibility, and letting users choose their own shortlink.
Assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, following a short link should be fast, pastes are text only, and page view analytics do not need to be realtime.
The primer assumes 10 million paste writes per month and 100 million paste reads per month, a 10:1 read to write ratio.
Each paste is 1 KB of content plus a record of shortlink 7 bytes, expiration_length_in_minutes 4 bytes, created_at 5 bytes and paste_path 255 bytes, about 1.27 KB in total.
That means 12.7 GB of new paste content per month, ~450 GB in 3 years, and 360 million shortlinks in 3 years. On average there are 4 paste writes per second and 40 read requests per second.

A relational database can act as a hash table mapping each url to the paste's file path, with an object store such as Amazon S3 holding the text. A NoSQL key-value store is the alternative; weigh SQL against NoSQL.

The pastes table's primary key is the shortlink, which builds an index the database uses to enforce uniqueness. A second index on created_at gives log-time lookups instead of a full scan and keeps the data in memory.
Clients use a public REST API, and internal services can talk to each other with Remote Procedure Calls.

A create request passes a reverse-proxy web server to the Write API server. It generates a unique url, retrying on a database duplicate, saves the row and the paste to the object store, and returns the url.

The url is the uniformly distributed MD5 hash of ip_address plus timestamp (or random data), Base 62 encoded since Base 64 adds + and /. The first 7 characters give 62^7 values, enough for 360 million shortlinks in 3 years.
A view request goes through the web server to the Read API server, which looks the url up in the SQL database. If found, it fetches the contents from the object store; otherwise it returns an error.

Since realtime analytics are not required, MapReduce over the web server logs can produce hit counts. Expired pastes are found by scanning the database for expiration timestamps older than now, then deleted or marked as expired.

Do not jump straight to the final design. Scale iteratively: load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. Ask what a load balancer with several web servers and master-slave replicas each fix.

For 40 average read requests per second (higher at peak), popular content is served from a memory cache, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. SQL read replicas handle cache misses unless busy replicating writes.

An object store such as Amazon S3 can handle 12.7 GB of new content per month. 4 average paste writes per second (more at peak) should suit a single SQL write master-slave; otherwise try federation, denormalization, SQL tuning or NoSQL.
